definition: A design principle in which a model is trained to prioritize instructions from certain sources (such as a system prompt) above others (such as content encountered while browsing), to resist prompt injection.
details: Instruction hierarchies aim to give models a principled way to weigh conflicting instructions from different sources, an important building block for safely deploying agents that process untrusted external content.

explainer.lead: An instruction hierarchy trains a model to rank instructions by source, putting a system prompt above content encountered while browsing. It is an important building block for safely deploying agents that process untrusted external content.

tiers.eli5: It is like teaching the model that some orders come from the boss and others from strangers, and the boss's orders win.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to give models a principled way to weigh conflicting instructions from different sources, chiefly as a defence against prompt injection. A pitfall is agents that process untrusted external content, where lower-priority text may still try to override the system prompt.
tiers.paperLevel: A design principle in which a model is trained to prioritise instructions from certain sources (such as a system prompt) above others (such as content encountered while browsing), to resist prompt injection. It aims to give models a principled way to weigh conflicting instructions from different sources.

explainer.example: A browser-reading agent encounters a web page telling it to ignore its system prompt; the hierarchy training keeps the system prompt in control.

citation.title: The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions
